720.bp: In real-world networks — social media, computer systems, financial transactions — most nodes are normal but a few are broken, malicious, or dangerous. We want to spot these outliers using only a handful of known good examples. The challenge: you can't just memorize what you've been shown; the network is complex, with hidden patterns in both the properties of nodes and how they're wired together.
720.wh: The usual approach to finding anomalies is to show a model one example of a 'bad' node and say 'find more like this.' But real anomalies don't come in one flavor. Some are slightly wrong, some are completely inverted, and some are a mix of both kinds of wrong simultaneously. A naive detector trained on a single corruption type will miss the nuanced, stepwise progression of how normal nodes decay into truly broken ones.
720.ap: This work proposes PAGE, which builds fake anomalies on purpose — but does it carefully, in stages. First, it takes known normal nodes and tweaks their numbers (attributes). Then it takes those tweaked nodes and rewires their connections in the graph, creating increasingly severe hybrid anomalies. Crucially, it trains the system to recognize that stepwise anomalies (mild corruption → severe corruption) form a progression, with harder anomalies clearly worse than easier ones.
720.ww: By learning to generate and rank this spectrum of corruption, the model builds a more complete picture of what 'wrong' looks like. Instead of having to memorize specific corruptions from labeled data, it learns the underlying logic: normal nodes sit at one end of a spectrum, and genuine anomalies are far along that spectrum. When a new, never-before-seen anomaly arrives, it's easier to spot because the model has internalized the rules of degradation.
720.po: On standard test graphs, PAGE beats existing methods significantly. The concrete gain is that it detects complex anomalies — nodes that mix attribute and structural corruption — which simpler approaches miss. This matters for real systems like fraud rings in financial networks, where bad actors disguise themselves by mixing strange transaction behavior with unusual connection patterns.

721.bp: News recommendation is about showing each person the articles they'll actually read, right now. But people's tastes shift constantly. A topic that mattered yesterday might be irrelevant tomorrow because a major event broke, the person got bored, or their life context changed. The system needs to track both what people stable like over months and what they crave in the next hour.
721.wh: Most systems freeze the social graph of past reads once and ask 'what's this person typically interested in?' This completely misses the oscillation of attention. A user might read politics every day for six weeks, then abandon it entirely for sports when a World Cup starts. A static snapshot can't see this shift without throwing out all the historical context that makes recommendations smart.
721.ap: This framework uses two branches running in parallel. One looks at the entire history to spot long-term patterns — 'this person loves tech news.' The other slices the recent past into chunks of time (stage-wise windows) and feeds them into an LSTM (a model that remembers sequences) to see the recent drift: 'they've been reading less tech this week.' It also uses attention to jump directly to the most relevant moments in the recent past, ignoring the noise.
721.ww: By combining long-term and short-term signals, the system avoids two failures. It doesn't over-fit to noise (short-term blips of unusual behavior) because it's anchored to what the person has reliably liked. It doesn't miss the signal either (the actual shift in interest) because it's explicitly listening to recent sequences. The two branches argue, and a smart combination of their outputs wins.
721.po: On real news recommendation logs from thousands of users, this framework delivers fresher, more relevant articles. The measurable win: when a user's interests shift (detected by the short-term branch), the recommendations adapt faster and remain less stale compared to pure long-term systems. This means fewer skipped articles and more engaged readers.

722.bp: Graph neural networks (machine learning models that learn patterns in networks) often fail when they have no information about nodes other than the wiring. Imagine trying to classify people in a social network if you only knew who knew whom, not their age, interests, or anything else. The network structure alone isn't enough; you need properties describing what each node is.
722.wh: Adding fake properties helps: if you pick a few representative nodes as 'landmarks' and measure how far every other node is from each landmark, you create a fingerprint. But which landmarks should you pick? How many? And which distance measure works best? These choices depend entirely on the specific graph and what you're trying to predict. No single choice works for all graphs.
722.ap: SCOUT learns these choices automatically. It tests different distance metrics (how to measure far-ness) and structure measures (e.g., 'hubs' or 'bridges') to find which pair works best for the given graph. It then uses the distribution of how central nodes are (the natural 'heavy tail' where a few nodes matter most) to automatically decide how many landmarks to use. Once these are tuned, it builds the fingerprints and feeds them into any graph neural network.
722.ww: Different graphs have different personalities. A social network favors landmarks that are hubs; a road network might favor nodes along bottlenecks. By learning graph-level properties first, SCOUT sidesteps the problem of hand-tuning per-graph. The heavy-tailed distribution insight captures the intuition that a few landmarks go a long way; adding the hundredth landmark helps far less than adding the second.
722.po: Across different tasks and graphs, SCOUT consistently improves performance without retuning. On link prediction in a drug-interaction network, it gains 26.88%. On node classification in a science paper network, it gains 4.52 accuracy points. Even when nodes already have properties, SCOUT's automatically chosen landmarks amplify the benefit, proving the method isn't solving a artificial problem.

723.bp: Online ads are sold by what happens after users click — do they buy, and if so, how much? Today most systems predict yes/no (did they convert?), but companies care about dollars, not just conversions. A click that leads to a $100 purchase is vastly more valuable than one that leads to a $5 purchase. The problem: the label (how much they spent) doesn't arrive instantly; it trickles in over hours or days as purchases complete.
723.wh: When labels arrive late, two things go wrong. First, the training data is constantly out of date — a model trained yesterday is already partially wrong because some old labels weren't complete. Second, users who make one big purchase look different from users who make many small purchases, but traditional models treat all purchases the same. A user who clicked and bought $5 five times is fundamentally different from a user who clicked once and bought $25.
723.ap: This work proposes READER, which routes incoming data to specialized experts depending on predicted behavior. If a user is predicted to repurchase (buy multiple times after a click), one expert handles them. If they're predicted to single-purchase, another expert takes over. These experts are trained separately on data where their behavior pattern clearly applies. Additionally, the system dynamically adjusts the target value during training — if you only saw a $10 purchase arrive but suspect more is coming, you adjust the label upward proportionally.
723.ww: This works because it acknowledges that predicting $100 from multi-purchase users is genuinely different than predicting $100 from single-purchasers. The features matter differently, the label distribution differs, and they benefit from different inductive bias. By separating them, each expert becomes specialized rather than confused. The dynamic calibration stops the system from systematically underestimating when data is incomplete.
723.po: On a newly introduced benchmark of real transaction sequences, READER outperforms methods that ignore the repurchase / single-purchase distinction. The concrete value: better GMV (gross merchandise volume) prediction means ad bidding becomes more accurate. An advertiser no longer overpays for users likely to single-purchase or underpays for repeat-purchase users; the model sees the difference.

724.bp: Implicit hate speech — messages that attack a group but hide the venom behind coded language, sarcasm, or metaphor — slips through automated filters that look only at words and tone. The real harm is in meaning that lives between the lines: 'those people really know how to dance' sounds innocent but, in context, is a slur. Catching this requires reading the intent underneath.
724.wh: Large language models often fail at this in a specific way: they pick up spurious cues (a curse word is present, so probably hateful) while missing the real semantic units that carry the slur (the coded reference, the sarcasm, the masked subject). Then they over-confident: they're certain they're right, even when they're completely wrong. The model is pseudo-reasoning — it sounds like it's thinking, but it's just pattern-matching to noise.
724.ap: DuPL is a two-stage framework. First, a 'Critical Miner' quickly scans the text to identify Latent Hate Components — the actual semantic building blocks that encode the slur. A 'Confusion Judge' steps in immediately if the message is unambiguous (explicitly hateful), short-circuiting to avoid wasted work. If the message is subtle, the second stage takes over: 'Deliberation' reasons about each LHC individually, building an argument for why this component is (or isn't) hateful, then integrates those arguments into a final judgment.
724.ww: This works because it decouples detection from reasoning. Most models try to do both at once and fail at both. By explicitly mining for the pieces that matter (LHCs), the system avoids pseudo-reasoning on red herrings. By reasoning component-wise, it can defend its conclusion; if an adversary knows which components the model fixates on, they can't fool it by changing a single surface cue.
724.po: Across three hate speech datasets, DuPL improves accuracy by 3.8 to 8.4 percentage points over prompt-based systems. Crucially, it lowers both false alarms and missed detections simultaneously — the model becomes more balanced. This matters for moderation: fewer false positives mean fewer innocent users suppressed; fewer false negatives mean fewer slurs slip through.

725.bp: Companies need to forecast multiple streams of data simultaneously — warehouse temperature and traffic flow, or electricity demand across buildings in a city. These streams interact in complex ways (when it rains, electricity demand and traffic flow both spike). But which forecasting algorithm should you use? Different algorithms excel on different streams and datasets; picking wrong wastes months of engineering time.
725.wh: Existing AutoML systems can't transfer knowledge between different time series datasets because they don't have a common language for describing them. A dataset with 1000 measurements per second looks nothing like one with 1 measurement per hour, even if the underlying patterns (seasonality, trend, noise) are structurally similar. Without that common language, every new dataset requires training from scratch.
725.ap: This work creates a large, labeled dataset (ModelPile) of 41 mainstream time series datasets across 11 domains, paired with the performance of 11 different forecasting algorithms. It then uses a large pre-trained model to compress each raw dataset into a universal code. On top of that code, a system called AutoMTSF asks: 'given the code of this new dataset, which algorithm will work best?' It treats algorithm selection as a classification problem — predict the winning algorithm — using patterns learned from ModelPile.
725.ww: The large pre-trained model acts as a universal translator: it turns any time series (fast or slow, seasonal or trend-driven) into a common representation. That representation preserves the essential properties but erases irrelevant details. Once you have that universal code, you can apply a classifier trained on thousands of algorithm-performance pairs; it has seen enough variety to generalize to a new time series it's never encountered.
725.po: On new datasets, AutoMTSF predicts which algorithm will win without training all of them. The concrete benefit: what used to take weeks (train 11 models, wait for each to converge) now takes minutes. For a company deploying forecasters across dozens of IoT sensors, this is the difference between monthly updates and real-time adaptivity.

726.bp: AI models trained on internet data inevitably memorize sensitive information — names, faces, private messages from people who didn't consent. When deployed, these models can be tricked into revealing what they memorized. The goal is to selectively erase memorized information from a model without breaking its ability to do useful work. The challenge: different tasks (answering questions, generating descriptions, filling in blanks) require different forgetting strategies.
726.wh: Most unlearning methods push the model to output garbage for a 'forget' class (e.g., 'never mention this person'). But that's brutal. If you indiscriminately garbage-collect, the model also forgets how to recognize the person in other contexts, or it starts refusing all similar tasks. You lose both sensitivity and utility. There's no single loss function that handles all the ways sensitive information leaks.
726.ap: TAU defines three task-aligned objectives corresponding to how the model is actually evaluated: classification (predict a category), free-form generation (write a description), and cloze (fill in a blank). For each, it crafts an unlearning loss. Classification uses confidence reduction (lower certainty on sensitive inputs). Generation uses controlled refusal (politely decline, don't spill). Cloze uses entity suppression (forget the association). All three are trained jointly with a 'retain' loss that preserves knowledge on non-sensitive examples.
726.ww: By matching the unlearning objective to the task, the model learns finer-grained forgetting. It doesn't just zero out a person's presence; it learns the distinction between refusing to classify the person, refusing to describe them, and refusing to complete sentences about them. This is more honest — it acknowledges that forgetting looks different depending on how you probe the model.
726.po: Across multiple multimodal models, TAU achieves more balanced unlearning. The measurable outcome: the model successfully forgets sensitive information (verification via adversarial probing), but retention accuracy on non-sensitive data remains high. For deployment, this means users can request deletion without fear of breaking the model's core capability.

727.bp: Internet-scale monitoring systems collect billions of data points per second — website latency, network traffic, sensor readings. Most data looks normal, but rare events (server outages, DDoS attacks, sensor failures) hide in that stream. Finding them is like looking for a needle in a haystack that's also moving and warping continuously. Speed and memory matter; you can't store everything or reprocess the entire history when a new anomaly arrives.
727.wh: Detecting anomalies in high-dimensional data (each data point has hundreds or thousands of features) is already hard. Add the constraint that it's streaming (you see each point once, then it's gone), and the data distribution keeps shifting (what's 'normal' today differs from yesterday), and the distribution is imbalanced (normal points vastly outnumber anomalies). Traditional methods either are too slow or confuse normal variations for true anomalies.
727.ap: ANN-TS uses Approximate Nearest Neighbor indexing — a technique that quickly finds the points most similar to the current point without checking every historical point. When a new data point arrives, it finds its neighbors in the stream. If neighbors are rare or far away (the point is isolated), that's a red flag. The system tracks a statistical score for each point based on its neighbors and uses an adaptive update strategy that gradually forgets old normal patterns as new patterns emerge.
727.ww: This works because anomalies are lonely — they have few similar points nearby. By asking 'how crowded is this point in its neighborhood?' you get a fast, interpretable signal. The approximate indexing keeps memory and computation low; you're not storing the full past. The adaptive update lets the system shift as the baseline changes; if network behavior evolves, the model tracks it.
727.po: On real web stream data, ANN-TS beats nine baseline methods, particularly when data is high-dimensional and skewed. The concrete benefit: companies can detect infrastructure anomalies in real time without expensive hardware or offline reprocessing. A sudden spike in latency or a surge in error rates is caught immediately.

728.bp: Bad actors — spammers, phishers, hate-mongers — disguise their messages by misspelling, using emojis, mixing alphabets, or other visual tricks: 'h@te,' 'ḥate,' '🅗ate'. Detection systems trained on clean text fail. The challenge is to decode the mangled text back to its original meaning fast enough for real-time moderation, without relying on massive models that are slow or brittle.
728.wh: Existing de-obfuscation methods rely on auto-regressive models (they predict one character at a time, like a typewriter) which are slow, or byte-level fallbacks, which are error-prone. When a message contains out-of-vocabulary symbols (unusual emojis or multi-code-point graphemes), these systems break down. They also can't fix a character in the middle of the word without reprocessing everything from the start.
728.ap: BIND (Bidirectionally Aligned Next-Token Denoising) works at the character level and aligns those characters bidirectionally — it looks at context from both directions simultaneously to decide what each garbled symbol should be. It uses a novel attention mechanism that fixes positions independently, not sequentially. This is like having multiple repair experts work on different parts of the sentence in parallel.
728.ww: By working bidirectionally and independently on each position, BIND achieves three wins: it's fast (no sequential generation), it handles out-of-vocabulary elements (they're just characters, not tokens in a vocabulary), and it's robust to variations. The model learns that 'h@te,' 'ḥate,' and '🅗ate' all map to the same target in different ways; the bidirectional context teaches it the pattern.
728.po: On obfuscated harmful text datasets, BIND outperforms larger models while being much faster. The real-world impact: moderators can use a small, task-specific model to clean messy text in milliseconds before feeding it to a hate-speech classifier. Companies achieve faster, cheaper, more reliable content moderation without scaling up to enormous models.

729.bp: In the real world, sensors are expensive and deployed sparsely — weather stations dot a region with gaps, but you need forecasts everywhere. This is called kriging: inferring values at unseen locations from observed ones using spatial and temporal structure. A city wants to know pollution levels everywhere, not just where monitors sit. The challenge: locations interact in complex ways, and the graph of relationships changes as conditions evolve.
729.wh: Older methods assume a static, predefined graph (e.g., 'use the 10 nearest neighbors'). But static graphs are brittle; they miss long-range dependencies and don't adapt when the data distribution shifts. Graph convolution networks iterate across the graph structure, but this is expensive and gets stuck in local patterns without a principled way to refine the target value based on feedback.
729.ap: DKM-GA combines diffusion (a technique that iteratively refines guesses) with graph-enhanced attention. It starts with an initial guess for the missing values, then uses attention to find the most relevant observed nodes (dynamically learning which nodes matter most, not just using static neighbors). It refines the guess using those relevant nodes. It repeats this process, each iteration getting feedback from the previous guess to update which nodes to trust.
729.ww: This works because diffusion is a natural fit for kriging: each iteration smooths and refines the guess. The graph-enhanced attention adapts the structure based on the refined values, not just static features. A node that initially looked relevant might become less important as the guess improves; the mechanism responds. The feedback loop (refined values → better attention → better refinement) is principled and stable.
729.po: On spatio-temporal prediction tasks (filling in missing weather measurements, sensor values in IoT networks), DKM-GA outperforms static-graph baselines. The concrete gain: predictions at unobserved locations become more accurate because the system dynamically identifies which observed locations actually matter for each missing location, adapting as conditions change.

730.bp: Graph neural networks learn representations by aggregating information from neighboring nodes, allowing them to recognize patterns in networks. But they have two scaling problems: computation explodes as graphs grow, and they struggle when tested on different graph types than they were trained on (out-of-distribution shift). A model trained on social networks might fail on citation networks, even though the structure is similar.
730.wh: Node-level attention (traditional approach) requires comparing every node to every potential neighbor, which is quadratic and infeasible on large graphs. More critically, node-level operations overfit to specific graph distributions; they learn surface patterns specific to the training graph rather than general principles about what makes a node important. The model becomes brittle.
730.ap: VecFormer introduces Vector Quantization to compress both node features and graph structure into discrete 'codes' — compact summaries capturing the essential information. Attention then operates on these codes (graph-token level) rather than individual nodes. Two separate codebooks learn what feature patterns matter and what structure patterns matter. This drastically reduces the computation (attending to a few dozen codes, not millions of nodes).
730.ww: The vector quantization acts as a lossy compression that forces the model to learn what truly matters, discarding noise. By working on codes rather than raw nodes, the model becomes less sensitive to surface variation; two graphs with the same structural and feature patterns get similar codes even if they differ in size or node ordering. This improves generalization. Computation drops because you're attending to summaries, not individuals.
730.po: On node classification tasks of various sizes, VecFormer beats existing graph transformers in both speed (especially on large graphs) and accuracy on out-of-distribution data. The concrete benefit: a single trained model generalizes across graph types without retraining, and inference is fast enough for real-time applications on million-node graphs.

731.bp: Recommendation systems often use knowledge graphs — structured data linking items, users, and concepts — to improve suggestions. A movie recommendation system might use a graph connecting movies to genres, actors, and themes. But real knowledge graphs are messy: some links are wrong, outdated, or irrelevant to recommendation. Noise in the graph corrupts the recommendations.
731.wh: Traditional recommendation systems treat the knowledge graph as given, noise and all. But the graph was built from various sources with different quality standards. A link that's true in general (this actor was in this movie) might be irrelevant for recommendation (the actor's presence doesn't actually predict user taste). Removing noise while keeping signal is hard; what looks like noise in isolation might matter when combined with other signals.
731.ap: This framework attacks the problem in two steps. First, Knowledge Filtering uses diffusion models to denoise the graph structure — gradually removing dubious connections while preserving strong ones. Second, Task-Specific Triplet Reconstruction identifies which remaining connections actually matter for recommendation by scoring them with attention and then retraining them using self-supervised learning (predicting the connection itself as a proxy for importance).
731.ww: The diffusion model is a natural fit for denoising: it iteratively refines the graph structure, trusting edges that remain stable and removing those that don't. The task-specific component prevents over-cleaning; rather than globally optimal, the system targets locally optimal — edges that are most useful for the recommendation task. Attention learns which triplets (user-item-concept relationships) matter; reconstruction forces the model to internalize why.
731.po: On recommendation datasets with noisy knowledge graphs, the framework produces cleaner graphs and better recommendations. The concrete benefit: users see more relevant suggestions because the graph no longer misleads the model with false or irrelevant connections. Recommendation diversity and accuracy both improve.

732.bp: Fraud in online services — fake transactions, misleading video chat, romance scams — is increasingly perpetrated by people modulating their emotional expressions strategically: faking sincerity, affecting a voice, adjusting facial micro-expressions. A fraud detector trained on static features (what was said) misses this emotional manipulation. The challenge: emotion is multimodal (visual, audio, text) and adversaries can coordinate their manipulation across all channels.
732.wh: Most fraud detectors treat emotions as static features to extract and forget. But emotions are signals that can be manipulated in coordinated ways. An adversary can perform micro-expressions while using specific vocal tones and word choices that all reinforce a false impression. Existing evaluations test single-mode attacks (only modify the face, or only the voice) and miss coordinated cross-modal attacks that an intelligent adversary would use.
732.ap: CEAT uses a Transformer-based architecture (which naturally handles multiple input modes) to jointly model emotional features (facial dynamics, vocal prosody) and semantic content (what's said). During training, it injects adversarial noise into the emotional latent space (the learned representation of emotions) in ways that respect context — the perturbation doesn't make the multimodal signals incoherent. This trains the model to be robust to emotional manipulation even when coordinated.
732.ww: By modeling emotion and context jointly, the system learns that emotional expressions should be consistent with semantic content. When an adversary tries to inject inconsistent emotional signals, the context-aware perturbation training makes the detector robust; the model has seen similar attacks and learned to ignore them. This is fundamentally different from testing single-modal perturbations — the model learns the pattern of cross-modal coherence.
732.po: On multimodal fraud detection benchmarks, CEAT withstands emotion-driven adversarial attacks better than baseline detectors. The concrete outcome: a fraudster trying to fake emotion across video, voice, and text is more likely to be caught because the system recognizes the incoherence. This makes emotion-based fraud more expensive and risky for perpetrators.

733.bp: Graph neural networks are deployed in real systems where the training data comes from one time period or one type of user, but the live system serves different users or different times. A fraud detector trained on 2024 data performs poorly in 2025 if fraud tactics shifted. This out-of-distribution problem undermines trust; predictions become overconfident and wrong. The system needs to know when it's unsure.
733.wh: Existing uncertainty methods are post-hoc: they guess uncertainty after the fact (e.g., disagreement across an ensemble) rather than learning where uncertainty arises from first principles. More critically, they can't explain why a prediction is unreliable — was it due to a missing feature, a shifted distribution, or genuine complexity? Without explanation, users can't trust the system in high-stakes decisions.
733.ap: SIGHT (Spiking Graph Predictive Coding) uses iterative error correction over graph structures. The model makes a prediction, then compares it to what it expects; the mismatch (error) is the core signal. If this error persists or grows across iterations, the system is confused — perhaps the distribution has shifted. These persistent mismatches become interpretable uncertainty signals. The 'spiking' mechanism makes errors explicit, visible to both the model and the user.
733.ww: This works because it recognizes that uncertainty has a source: distribution shifts cause persistent prediction errors. By exposing these errors iteratively, the model doesn't hide its confusion; it communicates it. A human expert can then ask: 'Why is the model uncertain here?' and get a concrete answer: 'The internal check found a persistent mismatch.' This transparency is crucial for high-stakes decisions.
733.po: On graph benchmarks with out-of-distribution scenarios, SIGHT improves both predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation simultaneously. The concrete benefit: a recommendation system or fraud detector can flag uncertain decisions for human review, preventing silent failures. Users gain interpretable explanations for why a decision might be untrustworthy.

734.bp: Imagine accessing the web through smart glasses that see the world you're seeing, hear what you're hearing, and understand what you need — without pulling out a phone or stopping what you're doing. For people with low vision, cognitive overload, or simply mobility constraints, this could be transformative. The challenge: understanding long, continuous first-person video (far longer than any model can process at once), parsing noisy speech, and seamlessly invoking web tools.
734.wh: A single neural network can't handle hours of video without extreme computational cost. Existing systems either truncate the context (losing long-horizon understanding) or batch-process offline (losing real-time responsiveness). Additionally, translating messy speech and gaze (where a person looks, often unreliable) into structured web commands requires multiple specialized models; running them all in real-time on glasses (with limited compute) is infeasible.
734.ap: Egocentric Co-Pilot uses a two-pronged approach. For reasoning, it combines Temporal Chain-of-Thought (reasoning step-by-step over time) with Hierarchical Context Compression (summarizing far-past events into memory, keeping only relevant context in the working window). This lets it answer complex questions over hours of video. For commands, it runs a lightweight multimodal intent layer that directly translates speech and gaze into structured commands, bypassing the need for a single monolithic model. It includes both cloud-native (WebRTC for low latency) and on-premise WebSocket deployments.
734.ww: Temporal reasoning works because it mirrors how humans think: they reason through a sequence and build summaries they can recall. By compressing older context, the system avoids forgetting but keeps computation manageable. The lightweight intent layer works because most speech/gaze commands are simple and predictable; a specialized small model beats a generalist large model. The dual-deployment approach lets users choose trade-offs (local privacy vs. cloud accuracy).
734.po: On egocentric video reasoning benchmarks, this system achieves competitive or better results than baselines while running on-device at real-time latency. The concrete impact: a person with low vision can ask their glasses 'what's on that menu?' or 'did I pass my exit?' and get an immediate, accurate answer without lifting their hands or stopping their activity. Web interaction becomes truly assistive.
